explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The psalm opens, "God is known in Judah; His name is great in Israel." God is known in Judah, and His name is great in Israel. I like a song that gets to the point before the first chorus.
Egypt never shows up anywhere in this psalm, friend. Asaph starts closer to home: "God is known in Judah; His name is great in Israel." Easy to grab a big famous name when you're guessing.

Moab isn't in this psalm, friend. The opening line says, "God is known in Judah; His name is great in Israel." So Judah is the place Asaph names first. The song stays with God's people right from the first line.

Zion it is! Verse 2 says, "His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion." Asaph names two places in that one verse, Salem for His tent and Zion for His dwelling place. Both are right there in the line.
Bethel doesn't appear in this psalm, friend. Asaph says, "His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion." So the second place is Zion. Good guess at a holy-sounding name, though.

Hebron isn't mentioned in this psalm, friend. The verse reads, "His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion." Hebron didn't make the guest list in that line, and I know how that feels. Zion is the answer.

Shattered! Verse 3 says, "There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war." Not bent, not dented, SHATTERED. When I drop a cookie tray, I get crumbs. Here it's the whole arsenal in pieces, and the psalm says God did it.

Nobody's collecting anything here, friend. The verse says, "There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war." Shattered is the word. Gathering them up would be a very different verse.

Hiding isn't what this verse says, friend. It says, "There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war." Shattered is what God did to them. Nothing in the verse has Him tucking them away.

Right, friend. Verse 4 says, "You are resplendent with light…" and Asaph is singing it straight to God. A few lines later he says, "…O God of Jacob…" so there's no doubt who he means. The song goes from talking ABOUT God to talking TO God.
Not quite, friend. The warriors show up in verse 5, and Asaph speaks of them as "they." The "You" in verse 4 is God, the One who is "…resplendent with light…" The song turns toward God first.

The kings come in at the very end, friend, in verse 12, where Asaph says God "…is feared by the kings of the earth." Asaph is talking about them there, not to them. The "You" in verse 4 is God, "…resplendent with light…"

That's it. Verse 4 says, "You are resplendent with light, more majestic than mountains filled with game." Mountains full of game are about as impressive as nature gets. And Asaph says God is MORE majestic than that.
Stars are a nice guess, friend, and I know a thing or two about stars in the sky. But this verse doesn't mention them. It says God is "…more majestic than mountains filled with game."

The sea doesn't come up in this verse, friend. Asaph says, "You are resplendent with light, more majestic than mountains filled with game." Waves are a mighty guess, and I'd have picked them too. But Asaph went with mountains.

Yes, plundered. Verse 5 says, "The valiant lie plundered; they sleep their last sleep." This is a heavy line, friend, and I think it's meant to be. These were brave men, and the verse says they were stripped of what they had.
Hidden isn't the word, friend. The verse says, "The valiant lie plundered; they sleep their last sleep." It's a heavy line, and I think we should just let it be heavy.

Honored isn't what the verse says, friend. It says, "The valiant lie plundered; they sleep their last sleep." It's a sobering picture of brave men who were stripped of what they had. The word is plundered.
The verse says the opposite, friend. Verse 5 ends, "No men of might could lift a hand." Men of might, and not one of them could lift a hand.
That's right, it's false. Verse 5 says, "No men of might could lift a hand." These were men of might, friend, and the verse says none of them could lift a hand.
His rebuke! Verse 6 says, "At Your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both horse and rider lie stunned." No weapons are mentioned there, friend. At His rebuke, horse and rider both lie stunned.
No whirlwind in this verse, friend. It says, "At Your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both horse and rider lie stunned." The rebuke is the whole cause. No weather needed.
Hailstones aren't in this verse, friend. Verse 6 says, "At Your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both horse and rider lie stunned." His rebuke is what the verse names.

That's not where the verse points, friend. Asaph first says, "You alone are to be feared." and then asks, "When You are angry, who can stand before You?" Nobody gets a brave-enough exemption in that line. Even the bravest person in the room, and I've seen a guy take a cookie from a hot tray with no mitt, can't stand before God's anger.

Right, it's false. Asaph says, "You alone are to be feared. When You are angry, who can stand before You?" The question points to this answer: no one can stand before God when He is angry. Being brave doesn't come into it.
Yes! Verse 8 says, "From heaven You pronounced judgment, and the earth feared and was still" Feared AND was still. The whole earth got quiet.
The earth doesn't roar here, friend. Verse 8 says it "…feared and was still" The quiet is what hits you. No shaking, just stillness.
Singing isn't what the verse says, friend. It says, "From heaven You pronounced judgment, and the earth feared and was still" The earth feared and was still, and it didn't sing out for joy.

explanations.answer: All the lowly of the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Verse 9 says God rose up to judge, "…to save all the lowly of the earth." ALL of them, friend. When God rises up, the lowly are on His mind.

Not this time, friend. Verse 9 says God rose up "…to save all the lowly of the earth." Princes come up in verse 12, where it says, "He breaks the spirits of princes…" The lowly are the ones named here.
Those aren't the ones named, friend. Verse 5 says of the men of might, "No men of might could lift a hand." Verse 9 says God rose up "…to save all the lowly of the earth."
Yes, it's true. Verse 10 says, "Even the wrath of man shall praise You…" Even human anger, Asaph says, shall praise God. That's a surprising line.
Asaph says it's true, friend. Verse 10 says, "Even the wrath of man shall praise You…" Even human anger ends up praising God. It's a surprising line, and it's right there in the psalm.
Vows! Verse 11 says, "Make and fulfill your vows to the LORD your God…" Making a promise is the easy part, friend. The psalm says to fulfill it too.
No battle plans here, friend. Verse 3 already says God shattered the weapons of war. Verse 11 says, "Make and fulfill your vows to the LORD your God…"
Altars aren't mentioned in this psalm, friend. Verse 11 says, "Make and fulfill your vows to the LORD your God…" It's about vows, meaning promises made and then kept.

Tribute is right. Verse 11 says, "let all the neighboring lands bring tribute to Him who is to be feared." The call goes out to all the neighboring lands, friend, not just one. Tribute is what they're told to bring.
Nobody's filing complaints here, friend. Verse 11 says, "let all the neighboring lands bring tribute to Him who is to be feared." Tribute is the word.

No soldiers in this verse, friend. It says, "let all the neighboring lands bring tribute to Him who is to be feared." The lands are told to bring tribute, not troops. Showing up with an army when you were asked for tribute? That would be a WILD plot twist.
Kings! Verse 12 says, "He breaks the spirits of princes; He is feared by the kings of the earth." Princes AND kings, friend. The ones who give the orders still fear Him.
Farmers don't show up here, friend. Verse 12 says, "He breaks the spirits of princes; He is feared by the kings of the earth." The psalm ends with the people at the top, the kings.

Sailors don't appear in this psalm, friend. The last verse says, "He breaks the spirits of princes; He is feared by the kings of the earth." Kings are the ones named. Even the folks at the top of the ladder fear Him.
